stories.title: Beavers filmed bonding after release in the wild
stories.summary: Conservationists are hopeful that two bonding beavers who were released into the wild earlier in 2026 could help to strengthen the population of the creatures. The beavers, which live on the Holnicote Estate, Exmoor, Somerset, were captured on trail cameras grooming each other. The semi-aquatic rodents were released in February as part of the National Trust's work to restore rivers, wetlands and floodplains on the 5,000-hectare site. National Trust ranger Mathieu Burtschell said: "The fact that they have paired up is a good indication that they have found the right conditions at Holnicote, with enough suitable habitat, food and space to establish a territory together." Beavers usually live in small family groups centred around an adult pair who then typically mate for life. Once the creatures establish their territory, their dams, canals and wetlands can help to create new habitats for other wildlife and keep water in the landscape for longer. Burtschell said the charity was hopeful the animals would explore, establish territories and start to form the relationships that were "so important" to a healthy beaver population. "Seeing these two beavers together on the trail camera is really exciting. "They are largely active at night, so trail cameras give us a valuable window into what they are doing when we are not there. "If the pair remains together, they could eventually establish their own family group and help strengthen the beaver population across the estate," he added. The beavers are being monitored by rangers to understand how they settle, move through the catchment and shape the surrounding habitat. They were among two groups that were released freely in Somerset for the first time, following a decision from the government to approve the reintroduction of the animals in England in 2025.

stories.title: Mansour Abbas is betting on a Zionist to make Arab votes count
stories.summary: Yoav Segalovich’s place on Raam’s slate is less about winning Jewish votes in the Israeli election than making Palestinian representation harder to exclude from coalition politics. Jewish participation in political lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel is not, in itself, unprecedented. Hadash was built around a Jewish-Arab political tradition and has for decades included Jewish candidates and lawmakers. Ofer Cassif sits in the Knesset today as one of its most outspoken Jewish members. What is distinctive about the Abbas-Segalovich arrangement is not that a Jew is running with an Arab list. It is the kind of Jewish political voice Abbas has chosen to place there: a Zionist former senior police commander whose political biography sits comfortably inside the Israeli mainstream, not outside it. Segalovich is joining Raam’s slate, not Raam itself, and the difference is easy to miss if one stops at the photograph. According to the arrangement, he will join the electoral list and parliamentary faction but will not become a member of the party. Raam’s constitution and internal decision-making structure will not change. Segalovich is also expected to retain the freedom to vote independently on questions where the ideological distance is obvious, including religion and state, security and LGBTQ rights. Abbas is not converting Raam into a Zionist party and Segalovich is not becoming an Islamist. They are testing whether two political identities that remain quite far apart can inhabit the same electoral vehicle.
